milestone: FtsZ & CetZ GTPase division rings (prokaryotic tubulin ancestor)
plain_title: A protein ring that pinches cells in two
plain_text: Bacteria and archaea have no walking motors, because random drifting crosses their tiny bodies in thousandths of a second. Instead they divide with FtsZ, a shrinking ring of protein blocks that is the ancestor of microtubules.
representative_system: Escherichia coli FtsZ & Haloferax volcanii CetZ
source: Löwe & Amos (1998) Nature 391:203; Osawa, Anderson & Erickson (2008) Science 320:792; Duggin et al. (2015) Nature 519:362
note: Conserved across bacteria and archaea, so inferred in or near the last universal common ancestor; single-monomer GTP hydrolysis curves the filament.

milestone: P-loop GTPase switches & AAA+ hexameric rings (motor enzyme precursors)
plain_title: Chemical switches and unfolding rings before walkers
plain_text: Long before any protein walked along a fiber, microbes used tiny phosphate-powered switches on the ribosome and six-part protein rings to unfold molecules. Complex cells later rebuilt those two parts into kinesin, myosin and dynein.
superfamily_or_track: P-loop NTPase switch & AAA+ ring superfamilies
representative_system: Ribosomal EF-Tu GTPase & prokaryotic MoxR AAA+ ring
source: Kull, Vale & Fletterick (1998) J. Muscle Res. Cell Motil. 19:877; Leipe et al. (2002) J. Mol. Biol. 317:41; Iyer et al. (2004) J. Struct. Biol. 146:11
note: Kinesin and myosin share their catalytic fold with small G-protein switches; dynein evolved independently from AAA+ ring chaperones.

plain_title: A spinning wheel set in the cell wall
plain_text: Swimming bacteria spin an outside corkscrew propeller with a true wheel-and-axle motor anchored in their membrane, powered by inward-flowing protons at up to 300 to 1,000 turns per second.
representative_system: Escherichia coli & Vibrio alginolyticus flagellar motor
source: Berg & Anderson (1973) Nature 245:380; Sowa & Berry (2008) Q. Rev. Biophys. 41:103
note: Driven by ~1,200 protons per revolution rather than ATP, and evolutionarily unrelated to the whip-like flagella of complex cells.

plain_title: A missing-link skeleton in complex life's host
plain_text: Asgard archaea, the closest relatives of the host cell that swallowed the mitochondrion, already build true proto-tubules from OdinTubulin and reach out slender arms using regulated actin fibers.
source: Zaremba-Niedzwiedzka et al. (2017) Nature 541:353; Akıl & Robinson (2018) Nature 562:439; Akıl et al. (2022) Sci. Adv. 8:eabm2225
note: Molecular-clock window for stem Asgard archaea prior to eukaryogenesis; no processive kinesin or dynein walkers exist in archaea.

plain_title: One-way hollow pipes that probe cellular space
plain_text: Duplicating proto-tubulin into alpha and beta halves built rigid 25-nanometer hollow pipes with a built-in arrow from cell center to edge, while growing tips search outward and snap back if they find nothing.
source: Mitchison & Kirschner (1984) Nature 312:237; Nogales, Wolf & Downing (1998) Nature 391:199; Desai & Mitchison (1997) Annu. Rev. Cell Dev. Biol. 13:83
note: Shared by all living complex cells, so present in their common ancestor before 1.65 billion years ago; depolymerizing protofilaments pull with ~30–65 pN.

milestone: Kinesin hand-over-hand plus-end walkers (escaping intracellular diffusion)
plain_title: Two-footed walkers that haul cargo outward
plain_text: Fueled by mitochondrial ATP, kinesin pairs two switch domains into feet that step hand over hand in 8-nanometer strides toward the cell edge—crossing a large cell in seconds instead of hours of random drifting.
representative_system: Kinesin-1 dimeric stepper (~11 families in LECA)
transport_regime: Ballistic linear transport (+ end, τ = L/v)
source: Vale, Reese & Sheetz (1985) Cell 42:39; Svoboda, Schmidt, Schnapp & Block (1993) Nature 365:721; Wickstead, Gull & Richards (2010) PLoS Biol. 8:e1000350
note: Phylogenomics reconstructs ~11 kinesin families already in the last eukaryotic common ancestor; step size and stall force measured by optical tweezers.

milestone: Cytoplasmic dynein minus-end AAA+ ring winches
plain_title: Giant ring winches that haul cargo back in
plain_text: To bring packets and signals back from the cell rim to the nucleus, complex cells fused six chaperone rings into one giant heavy chain with a long stalk that winches cargo inward along microtubules.
superfamily_or_track: Dynein heavy chain (6× AAA+ ring motor)
transport_regime: Ballistic linear transport (− end, τ = L/v)
source: Paschal & Vallee (1987) Nature 330:181; Carter, Cho, Jin, Vale & Burgess (2011) Science 331:1159; Reck-Peterson et al. (2018) Nat. Rev. Mol. Cell Biol. 19:382
note: Cytoplasmic and ciliary dyneins had already diverged before the last common ancestor of complex cells.

milestone: Myosin walkers on actin fibers (crawling, phagocytosis & cytokinesis)
plain_title: Actin walkers for crawling and swallowing
plain_text: Built from the same ancient switch fold as kinesin, myosin motors pull on thin actin cables near the cell skin to swallow food particles, crawl over surfaces and pinch dividing cells.
representative_system: Myosin V cargo walker & Myosin II contractile filament
source: Kull et al. (1996) Nature 380:550; Mehta et al. (1999) Nature 400:590; Richards & Cavalier-Smith (2005) Nature 436:1113
note: At least three myosin classes trace to the common ancestor of complex cells; animals later arrayed Myosin II into striated muscle.

milestone: Bipolar mitotic spindle & kinetochore chromosome segregation
plain_title: A mechanical sorter that protects big genomes
plain_text: Once DNA grew into many separate chromosomes, random splitting would lose genes at every division. Opposing kinesin and dynein motors balance shrinking microtubule tips to deal an exact copy of every chromosome to each daughter cell.
source: Kapitein et al. (2005) Nature 435:114; Akiyoshi et al. (2010) Nature 468:576; McIntosh, Volkov & Ataullakhanov (2012) Q. Rev. Biophys. 45:147
note: Breaks the segregation error ceiling so genomes could scale from millions to billions of DNA letters.

milestone: 9+2 motile cilium, axonemal dynein waves & intraflagellar transport
plain_title: Whip-like oars that steer cells and become animal sensors
plain_text: Nine pairs of microtubules arranged in a cylinder slide past each other when dynein arms pull, beating 50 times a second to steer green algae toward light—and later evolving into the light-catching tips of our own eye rods and cones.
superfamily_or_track: 9+2 microtubule axoneme + axonemal dynein + kinesin-2 IFT
transport_regime: Doublet sliding bending waves + IFT elevator trains
source: Summers & Gibbons (1971) PNAS 68:3092; Kozminski, Johnson, Forscher & Rosenbaum (1993) PNAS 90:5519; Moran, Rowley & Zakon (2014) Mol. Biol. Evol. 31:2464
note: 2.5 µm/s is intraflagellar transport elevator speed inside the cilium (whole-cell ciliary swimming reaches ~100–1,000 µm/s); the 9+2 cilium itself goes back to LECA.

milestone: Meiotic chromosome-pairing bouquet & two-step reduction spindle
plain_title: Dynein shakes the nucleus so matching chromosomes meet
plain_text: For sex to shuffle two parents' genes without scrambling them, matching chromosomes must find each other inside a crowded nucleus. Dynein motors drag chromosome ends back and forth to pair homologs before two spindle divisions halve the set.
superfamily_or_track: Nuclear-envelope dynein LINC bouquet + meiotic spindle
source: Chikashige et al. (1994) Science 264:270; Butterfield (2000) Paleobiology 26:386; Ramesh, Malik & Logsdon (2005) Curr. Biol. 15:185
note: Anchored to Bangiomorpha (~1.05 Ga), the oldest fossil showing sexual spore tetrads; core meiotic genes trace to LECA.

milestone: Long-distance microtubule endosome shuttles in fungal hyphae
plain_title: Nonstop supply trains to the tips of fungal threads
plain_text: Fungal threads tunnel across centimeters or meters by adding new wall only at their very tip. Kinesin-3 and dynein run continuous cargo shuttles along microtubule tracks so distant tips never starve.
source: Seiler et al. (1997) EMBO J. 16:3025; Steinberg (2007) Nat. Rev. Microbiol. 5:509; Loron et al. (2019) Nature 570:232
note: Fossil date from Arctic chitinous fungal microfossils (~0.9–1.0 Ga); shuttle speeds measured in living filamentous fungi.

milestone: Polarized axonal microtubule highways & dendritic input/output asymmetry
plain_title: Microtubule highways that keep long nerve fibers alive
plain_text: A synapse protein drifting at random would take 1,585 years to travel down a one-meter nerve fiber. Axons point every microtubule outward so kinesin delivers fresh synapse parts in days and dynein brings survival signals home—while mixed directions mark input dendrites.
superfamily_or_track: Uniform + end axonal microtubules (Tau/MAPs) + Kinesin-1/3 & Dynein
representative_system: Bilaterian motor & sensory axons (squid loligo / vertebrate)
source: Brady (1985) Nature 316:73; Baas, Deitch, Black & Banker (1988) PNAS 85:8335; Hirokawa, Niwa & Tanaka (2010) Neuron 68:610
note: Dated to the earliest bilaterian fossils (~555 Ma); fast synaptic-vesicle kinesin-3 (KIF1A) reaches ~2–5 µm/s (~200–400 mm/day).

milestone: The enzymatic tubulin code & activity-dependent synaptic cargo routing
plain_title: Chemical road signs on tracks steer memory supplies
plain_text: Enzymes write chemical tags onto microtubule tails that work as classical road signs, steering specific kinesins and receptor packets into active nerve branches and spines—whereas proposed room-temperature quantum states in microtubules fade in picoseconds.
superfamily_or_track: Tubulin tail modification code + KIF1A/KIF5 + spine Myosin V
source: Verhey & Gaertig (2007) J. Cell Sci. 120:4119; Janke & Magiera (2020) Nat. Rev. Mol. Cell Biol. 21:307; Tegmark (2000) Phys. Rev. E 61:4194
note: In warm salty cytosol (Debye screening ~0.8 nm, water relaxation ~8.3 ps), quantum coherence collapses ~10^9 times faster than neural spikes; microtubules contribute to cognition via classical routing and structural polarity.

milestone: Ultra-fast plant Myosin XI cytoplasmic streaming
plain_title: High-speed plant motors stir giant vacuolated cells
plain_text: Land plants and their green-algal relatives grow giant cells while losing dynein motors. Instead, plant Myosin XI—the fastest biological walker known—sprints along actin cables at up to 50 micrometers a second, stirring the whole cell like a conveyor belt.
superfamily_or_track: Plant Myosin XI on cortical F-actin bundles
representative_system: Chara corallina internodal cells & Arabidopsis Myosin XI
source: Kamiya & Kuroda (1956) Bot. Mag. Tokyo 69:544; Ito et al. (2007) Biochem. Biophys. Res. Commun. 312:958; Tominaga et al. (2013) Dev. Cell 27:345
note: Reaches ~50–60 µm/s in charophyte green algae and ~7 µm/s in flowering plants, which lost both cytoplasmic dynein and motile cilia.
